Sometimes the malaprops of the

the news pages and nightly news
(Was it wet or white or what?), but
more often they reached a snick-
ering press corps and were allowed
to dic a dignified death.

After all, this is a city where
Mayor Richard J. Daley’s press
secretary, Earl Bush, once ad-
monished reporters; “Don’t write
what he says, write what he
means.”

Sometimes, it took great
scratching of noggins to find the
grain of syntax in some of the ut-
terings during the 1989 campaign,
such as the day when Richard M.
Daley was speaking at a forum
sponsored by the National Organi-
zation for Women and tried to
summarize his views on abortion
and birth control.
This is the 1990s, We cannot
close our eyes or run in the closet,
Huh?
Richiespeak drew the most atten-
tion on the campaign trail, since he
alone inherited a legacy of frac-
tured sentences from his father.
But there was Mayor Eugene
Sawyer, trying to impress a group

And-there was Ed Vrdolyak dem-
onstrating how easy it would be to
write his name on the Republican
ballot for mayor by spelling the of-
fice in big letters: “M-A-R-O-R.”
And there was Ald. Timothy
Evans (4th), who found some un-
usual comparisons to Harold
Washington when he tried to ex-
plain why he used the late mayor’s
name for his political party:
J took a position that if elephants
can symbolize Republicans, if a
Jackass can symbolize the Demo-
crats, then certainly what Harold
Washington stood for could sym-
bolize a party.
And Daley again, complaining
within earshot of a Wall Street
Journal reporter that Sawyer used
someone else to speak in his politi-
cal ads.
He has James Earl Ray.
Now that would be a story. But
it was actor James Earl Joncs, not

‘the convicted murderer of Dr.

Martin Luther King Jr., who spoke
on Sawyer’s ads. A correction from
a Daley aide elicited the mayor-
elect’s soon-to-be-famous giggle.
The trouble for candidates here
who stumble over the English
language is that when a Chicago
mayor speaks, he can fire the shot
misheard around the world.
New Yorkers who might have
missed the Journal could’ count
on the New York Times, which

Then there were the campaign

ganizer Robert Lucas who ex-
plained why Evans would be a

Well, they were trying. Daley-has
used a Northwestern University
professor as a speech coach several
times in his political career, and
Sawyer sought similar assistance
from a public relations firm to ar-
ticulate away his “Mayor Mum-
bles” nickname. Dalcy even tried
to pre-empt criticism by airing a
commercial that declared he wasn’t
a very good speaker.

“You counsel them to think be-
fore they speak and concentrate on
the message they’re trying to pro-
mote so they don’t get issues that
might take them into uncharted
and dangerous waters,” said David
Axelrod, the media meister who
created the Daley ads.

“He isn’t the most elegant speak-
er, but he’s not prone to many
mistakes that blow up on you,”
Axelrod said. “When } worked for
Harold [Washington], he was so
ebullient that there was no con-
taining him. He was a quote ma-
chine, and occasionally a word that
was completely foreign to the Eng-
lish language would find its way
in.”
Sometimes the words all fit in
the right place during the mayoral
race, but sounded awfully strange
anyway. There was, for cxample,
Ald. Lawrence Bloom (5th), the

earnest independent who cam- _

paigned a while in the Democratic . -

._ Make no mistake about it. I am
in this race to stay.
That was Bloom, announcing his
candidacy.
By golly, I still have a chance at
it. I’m not going to quit. I got in
and I’m going to stay in. It’s not
always pleasant, but it’s always
necessary.
That was Bloom, 20 hours before
he announced that it wasn’t so
necessary that he run for mayor.
No, of course not.
That was Bloom, asked whether
he intended to quit the mayor’s
race 10 hours before he quit.
Chicago deserves better than
Gene Sawyer.

Bloom again, before he heartily
endorsed Sawyer for mayor.
Fortunately for the candidates,
the fractured facts and malaprops
often go unchallenged by the press.
Unfortunately for the candidates,
they sometimes venture onto the
risk-laden ground of live television,
where they can run at the mouth,
but they can’t hide.
And in that spirit, Sawyer,
battling a wishy-washy image for
the whole campaign, flatly told
thousands watching a live debate:
There’s no decisiveness on my

And Daley, who tried to explain

There aren’t any race issucs in
